question: What is the Bonferroni correction and what per-test threshold results from 5 tests at alpha 0.05?
answer: The Bonferroni correction per-test threshold for 5 tests at alpha 0.05 is 0.01 [S1].

citations.title: Statistics Lab Report Guide
citations.text:
Lab Report Checklist
Every lab report states the sample size n, the sample mean, the sample standard deviation and a 95% confidence interval. Use alpha = 0.05 unless the lab sheet states otherwise. Always report the exact p-value rather than only writing p < 0.05.
When several hypotheses are tested on the same data, apply a Bonferroni correction: divide alpha by the number of tests m. With 5 tests and alpha = 0.05 each individual test is judged against 0.01.

S3.title: Statistics Estimators And Bias
S3.text:
3. The Bootstrap
The bootstrap estimates the uncertainty of a statistic by resampling. Draw n observations with
replacement from the original sample of size n, compute the statistic, and repeat this B times, for
example B = 1000. The spread of the B statistics approximates the sampling variability.
A bootstrap percentile interval for 95% confidence uses the 2.5th and the 97.5th percentiles of the
B bootstrap statistics. The bootstrap needs no formula for the standard error, which makes it useful
for medians and other awkward statistics.

S5.text:
L2 regularization and early stopping
3. Early stopping Early stopping monitors validation loss during training and stops when it has not
improved for a fixed number of epochs (the patience); the best checkpoint is restored. Advantages:
it needs no change to the model, saves training compute, and the stopping epoch acts as an
implicit regularizer. Disadvantages: it requires a held-out validation set that is then not used for
training, results are sensitive to the patience value, and noisy validation curves can trigger a
premature stop. 4. Dropout Dropout randomly zeroes a fraction p of hidden units at each training
step so units cannot co-adapt. It is applied only during training. It is mainly used for neural
networks.

S6.title: Statistics Exercise Guide
S6.text:
Problem 4: One-Sample Hypothesis Test
Question. A factory claims bulbs last 1000 hours on average. A sample of 25 bulbs has mean 980 and sample standard deviation 50. Test H0: mu = 1000 against H1: mu is not 1000 at alpha = 0.05.
Solution. The t statistic is (980 - 1000) / (50 / sqrt(25)) = -20 / 10 = -2.0 with 24 degrees of freedom. The two-sided critical value is about 2.064. Because the absolute value 2.0 is smaller than 2.064 we fail to reject H0 at the 5% level. Failing to reject does not prove the claim is true; the sample may simply lack the power to detect a 20 hour difference.

S7.title: Statistics Lecture Notes
S7.text: 5. Hypothesis Testing Hypothesis testing evaluates a claim about a population. The null hypothesis H0 states no effect or no difference; the alternative hypothesis H1 states the effect we are looking for. We compute a test statistic from the sample and a p-value, the probability of observing a result at least as extreme as the one found, assuming H0 is true. If the p-value is smaller than the significance level alpha, commonly 0.05, we reject H0. A Type I error means rejecting a true null hypothesis, and its probability is alpha. A Type II error means failing to reject a false null hypothesis, with probability beta. Power equals 1 - beta, the probability of detecting a real effect. Larger samples increase power. A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and a small p-value does not measure the size or importance of an effect.
